title: Spiritual communion
hookLine: when you can't receive, you can ask to be united in desire

cards: Spring 2020. Churches around the world locked their doors. Millions of Catholics who had received Communion every Sunday of their lives were suddenly watching Mass on a laptop at the kitchen table.
The priest held up the host on a grainy screen, and there was nothing to walk forward to. Many of them, at that moment, did something their grandparents knew well but they had barely heard of.
They closed their eyes and asked to receive him anyway, without bread.

teach.b: Spiritual communion is the old Catholic practice of uniting yourself to Jesus in the Eucharist by desire, when you can't receive him in the sacrament. It isn't new, and it isn't only for emergencies.
The Council of Trent, in the 1500s, spoke of people who receive spiritually, eating by desire, through a living faith.
Thomas Aquinas taught that the effect of the sacrament can be received by desire, the way a person who longs for baptism is already turned toward it. Who uses it?

teach.h: THE SICK, THE FAR, THE WAITING.
teach.b: The sick who can't get to church. People in places with no priest. Those who, for reasons of Church teaching, aren't able to receive Communion at a given time: they can still come to Mass and make a spiritual communion.
Non-Catholics at a Catholic Mass sometimes do this too, in their own way. And many Catholics make one every day, at home, outside of Mass. Saints have loved it.
Alphonsus Liguori, an eighteenth-century Italian bishop, wrote a short prayer for it that's still widely used.

In essence: I believe you are present in the Blessed Sacrament; I love you above all things and desire to receive you; since I can't now receive you sacramentally, come at least spiritually into my heart; I embrace you as if you were already there, and never let me be separated from you.
Catholics are clear it isn't the same as receiving the sacrament.
It's a longing, not a substitute. But they also say longing is not nothing.
A desire turned toward God is already a kind of opening. That's the week in adoration: the tabernacle, the monstrance, the holy hour, Benediction, and now this.

how: Catholics who can't receive Communion, whether sick, far from a church, or not able to receive at a given Mass, often make a spiritual communion, many using Alphonsus Liguori's short prayer or their own words.

o: receiving Communion at a Mass you watch online
joining yourself to Jesus in the Eucharist by longing
a feeling of closeness at a church retreat

games.q: what's inside the practice — tap the pairs.
p: churches locked, Mass on a laptop

s: spiritual communion was invented during the 2020 lockdowns
it's centuries old; Trent and Aquinas both taught it.
Catholics say it's the same as receiving the sacrament
it's a longing, not a substitute, though a real opening to God.
it can be made at home, outside of Mass
many Catholics make one every day.

games.q: you're at Mass, but for a reason of Church teaching you can't receive Communion today. what can you do?
o: stay, and make a spiritual communion.
go forward anyway and hope no one notices.
games.why: the Church encourages staying and uniting yourself by desire. many also go forward with arms crossed for a blessing.

practice: If you're Catholic, use Alphonsus Liguori's prayer if you know it, or say the same thing simply in your own words: that you believe, that you long for him, and that you ask him to come into your heart; then stay quiet, as you would after receiving.
If you're not Catholic, think of something or someone you long for but can't reach right now, and notice that the longing itself is a kind of closeness.

wordCard.voice: Spiritual communion. Uniting yourself to Jesus in the Eucharist by desire, when you can't receive him in the sacrament. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: desire is a door. Tomorrow, the liturgical year begins. That's day one hundred forty-two.
